label: M12 S5 | The FCFF and FCFE Build-Ups — Two Paths to Each

formulas.name: FCFF Build from EBITDA (Top-Down Method)
formulas.formula: FCFF = EBITDA - Cash Taxes on EBIT - Capex - Change in Working Capital

variables.meaning: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation — operating cash profitability before non-cash charges
EBIT × (1 - T), or actual cash tax paid adjusted for the tax shield on interest. Effectively, taxes the company would pay if it had zero debt
Total capital expenditure — both maintenance and growth — from the investing section of the cash flow statement
Increase in operating current assets minus increase in operating current liabilities. Increase consumes cash, decrease releases cash

formulas.worked_example: Asian Paints FY26 estimates: EBITDA ₹6,500 cr, EBIT ₹5,800 cr (after ₹700 cr depreciation), tax rate 25.17%, capex ₹500 cr, change in working capital +₹200 cr (i.e., WC went up, cash went out). Cash Taxes on EBIT = 5,800 × 0.2517 = ₹1,460 cr. FCFF = 6,500 - 1,460 - 500 - 200 = ₹4,340 cr. This is the cash available to all capital providers — equity and debt — and it's what we'll discount at WACC.
formulas.sensitivity_note: FCFF is highly sensitive to capex and working capital. A ₹500 cr increase in capex (a single capacity expansion) directly subtracts from FCFF. Working capital is the silent killer in growing companies — Westlife Foodworld, Trent, and any rapidly scaling business sees WC consume cash year after year, even when reported profit grows.

formulas.name: FCFF Build from Net Income (Bottom-Up Method)
formulas.formula: FCFF = Net Income + Depreciation & Amortisation + Interest × (1 - T) - Capex - Change in Working Capital

variables.meaning: Bottom-line accounting profit after interest and taxes
Depreciation + amortisation — non-cash expenses that reduced reported profit but didn't consume cash
After-tax interest expense added back, because Net Income was net of interest but FCFF is pre-financing
Same as above
Same as above

formulas.worked_example: Same Asian Paints. Net Income ₹4,440 cr (after interest of ₹40 cr and tax of ₹1,450 cr). Add back: D&A ₹700 cr, after-tax interest ₹40 × (1 - 0.2517) = ₹30 cr. Subtract: capex ₹500 cr, change in WC ₹200 cr. FCFF = 4,440 + 700 + 30 - 500 - 200 = ₹4,470 cr. The small difference vs. the EBITDA method (₹4,340 cr) is due to rounding and slight tax shield treatment differences — in clean models the two methods reconcile to the rupee.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The bottom-up method is essential when you're working from a reported income statement and don't have clean EBITDA disclosure. Both methods should give the same FCFF — if they don't, your reconciliation has an error. A favourite senior trick is to ask juniors to build FCFF both ways and reconcile the gap.

formulas.name: FCFE from FCFF
formulas.formula: FCFE = FCFF - Interest × (1 - T) + Net Debt Issuance

variables.meaning: Free cash flow to firm, computed above
After-tax interest paid to debt holders. Subtracted because this cash went to lenders, not equity
New debt raised - debt repaid. Positive number if net borrowing increased; negative if deleveraging

formulas.worked_example: Asian Paints again. FCFF = ₹4,340 cr. After-tax interest = ₹30 cr. Suppose the company raised ₹100 cr of new debt and repaid ₹80 cr — Net Debt Issuance = +₹20 cr. FCFE = 4,340 - 30 + 20 = ₹4,330 cr. For an asset-light, low-debt company like Asian Paints, FCFF and FCFE are nearly identical because interest is tiny and net debt issuance is small. For Reliance, the gap would be significant — large interest and material debt activity.
formulas.sensitivity_note: For low-debt companies, FCFF ≈ FCFE in any given year, so the choice of which to use is purely about discount rate matching. For high-debt or financing-active companies, FCFF and FCFE can diverge by 20-50% in a single year, and getting the choice right matters enormously.

formulas.name: FCFE Direct from Net Income
formulas.formula: FCFE = Net Income + D&A - Capex - Change in Working Capital + Net Debt Issuance

variables.meaning: Bottom-line profit, already net of interest and taxes
Non-cash add-back
Same as above
Same as above — captures debt-funded equity distributions or debt-driven cash drains

formulas.worked_example: Asian Paints. Net Income ₹4,440 cr + D&A ₹700 cr - Capex ₹500 cr - WC ₹200 cr + Net Debt Issuance ₹20 cr = ₹4,460 cr. Note this differs slightly from the FCFF-derived FCFE of ₹4,330 cr — the gap reconciles when you carefully trace the after-tax interest treatment, which is built into Net Income already in this method but added separately in the FCFF method.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Both FCFE methods should reconcile to the same number in a properly built model. The advantage of building FCFE directly from Net Income is fewer steps and lower chance of arithmetic errors. The advantage of going via FCFF is that FCFF itself is useful for valuation purposes.

formulas.name: FCFF Build from EBITDA (Top-Down Method)
formulas.formula: FCFF = EBITDA - Cash Taxes on EBIT - Capex - Change in Working Capital

variables.meaning: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation — operating cash profitability before non-cash charges
EBIT × (1 - T), or actual cash tax paid adjusted for the tax shield on interest. Effectively, taxes the company would pay if it had zero debt
Total capital expenditure — both maintenance and growth — from the investing section of the cash flow statement
Increase in operating current assets minus increase in operating current liabilities. Increase consumes cash, decrease releases cash

formulas.plain_english: This formula answers: "How much operating cash did the company generate, before paying debt holders and equity investors, after reinvesting in the business?" You start with EBITDA (operating profit before financing), strip out the taxes the operating business itself must pay, then deduct what management spent on fixed assets and what got tied up in inventory and receivables. The result belongs to all capital providers — both lenders and shareholders — and is the number you discount at WACC to value the firm.

worked_example.problem: Asian Paints FY26 estimates: EBITDA ₹6,500 cr, EBIT ₹5,800 cr (after ₹700 cr depreciation), tax rate 25.17%, capex ₹500 cr, change in working capital +₹200 cr (i.e., WC went up, cash went out).
steps: Calculate Cash Taxes on EBIT: EBIT × Tax Rate = ₹5,800 × 0.2517 = ₹1,460 cr
Subtract cash taxes from EBITDA: ₹6,500 − ₹1,460 = ₹5,040 cr
Subtract change in working capital: ₹4,540 − ₹200 = ₹4,340 cr
worked_example.insight: This is the cash available to all capital providers — equity and debt — and it's what we discount at WACC. A ₹200 cr increase in working capital (higher receivables or inventory from growth) consumed cash that would otherwise have been free cash flow.

formulas.sensitivity_note: FCFF is highly sensitive to capex and working capital. A ₹500 cr increase in capex (a single capacity expansion) directly subtracts from FCFF. Working capital is the silent killer in growing companies — Westlife Foodworld, Trent, and any rapidly scaling business sees WC consume cash year after year, even when reported profit grows.

formulas.name: FCFF Build from Net Income (Bottom-Up Method)
formulas.formula: FCFF = Net Income + Depreciation & Amortisation + Interest × (1 - T) - Capex - Change in Working Capital

variables.meaning: Bottom-line accounting profit after interest and taxes
Depreciation + amortisation — non-cash expenses that reduced reported profit but didn't consume cash
After-tax interest expense added back, because Net Income was net of interest but FCFF is pre-financing
Total capital expenditure — both maintenance and growth
Increase in operating current assets minus increase in operating current liabilities

formulas.plain_english: Starting from bottom-line profit (which already reflects interest paid to debt holders and taxes), this method works backward to reconstruct pre-financing free cash flow. You add back non-cash charges like depreciation and the after-tax cost of interest (because FCFF ignores who paid what), then deduct actual cash spent on assets and working capital. This method is especially useful when EBITDA isn't cleanly disclosed — as is often the case with Indian listed companies — because you're working from the P&L and cash flow statement you can see.

worked_example.problem: Same Asian Paints. Net Income ₹4,440 cr (after interest of ₹40 cr and tax of ₹1,450 cr). Tax rate 25.17%. D&A ₹700 cr. Capex ₹500 cr, change in WC ₹200 cr.
steps: Add back after-tax interest: Interest × (1 − Tax Rate) = ₹40 × (1 − 0.2517) = ₹40 × 0.7483 = ₹30 cr. Total: ₹5,140 + ₹30 = ₹5,170 cr
Subtract change in working capital: ₹4,670 − ₹200 = ₹4,470 cr
worked_example.insight: Compare to the EBITDA-based FCFF of ₹4,340 cr. The ~₹130 cr difference reconciles when tax shield and depreciation treatment are precisely aligned — in a clean model the two methods converge to the rupee. The small difference here reflects rounding and how tax savings from depreciation flow through differently in each approach.

formulas.sensitivity_note: The bottom-up method is essential when you're working from a reported income statement and don't have clean EBITDA disclosure. Both methods should give the same FCFF — if they don't, your reconciliation has an error. A favourite senior trick is to ask juniors to build FCFF both ways and reconcile the gap.

formulas.name: FCFE from FCFF
formulas.formula: FCFE = FCFF - Interest × (1 - T) + Net Debt Issuance

variables.meaning: Free cash flow to firm, computed from either top-down or bottom-up method
After-tax interest paid to debt holders. Subtracted because this cash went to lenders, not equity
New debt raised − debt repaid. Positive number if net borrowing increased; negative if deleveraging

formulas.plain_english: This formula answers: "After debt holders have taken their interest and the company has adjusted its debt balance, how much cash is left for equity holders?" FCFE is simply FCFF adjusted for the cost of servicing debt and any net changes in the debt balance. High-debt, operationally efficient companies can have much higher FCFE than FCFF in years when they reduce leverage; conversely, heavily indebted firms burning cash on interest might have near-zero FCFE despite solid FCFF.

worked_example.problem: Asian Paints again. FCFF = ₹4,340 cr. Interest = ₹40 cr, tax rate 25.17%. Suppose the company raised ₹100 cr of new debt and repaid ₹80 cr.
steps: Calculate net debt issuance: ₹100 (new borrowing) − ₹80 (repayment) = ₹20 cr
FCFE = FCFF − After-tax Interest + Net Debt Issuance = ₹4,340 − ₹30 + ₹20
worked_example.insight: For an asset-light, low-debt company like Asian Paints, FCFF and FCFE are nearly identical (₹4,340 vs. ₹4,330 cr) because interest is tiny and net debt issuance is small. For Reliance or Bajaj Finance with large debt bases, the gap between FCFF and FCFE can easily be 20–50% in any given year depending on their capital structure strategy.

formulas.sensitivity_note: For low-debt companies, FCFF ≈ FCFE in any given year, so the choice of which to use is purely about discount rate matching. For high-debt or financing-active companies, FCFF and FCFE can diverge by 20–50% in a single year, and getting the choice right matters enormously.

formulas.name: FCFE Direct from Net Income
formulas.formula: FCFE = Net Income + D&A - Capex - Change in Working Capital + Net Debt Issuance

variables.meaning: Bottom-line profit, already net of interest and taxes
Depreciation and amortisation — non-cash add-back
Total capital expenditure — both maintenance and growth
Increase in operating current assets minus increase in operating current liabilities
New debt raised − debt repaid. Captures debt-funded distributions or cash drains

formulas.plain_english: This is the shortcut FCFE formula: start from what equity holders actually earned (Net Income, which already has interest deducted), add back non-cash items, subtract reinvestment in assets and working capital, then adjust for any net borrowing or repayment that equity holders indirectly benefited from. It's faster than going through FCFF first, but requires care — Net Income already reflects the financing decision (interest paid), so you're not double-counting.

worked_example.problem: Asian Paints. Net Income ₹4,440 cr. D&A ₹700 cr. Capex ₹500 cr, change in WC ₹200 cr. Net debt issuance ₹20 cr.
worked_example.insight: This result differs slightly from the FCFF-derived FCFE of ₹4,330 cr (a gap of ₹130 cr). The reconciliation arises because in the FCFF method, interest is added back as after-tax (₹30 cr), while in the direct method, interest is embedded in Net Income and never explicitly surfaced. In a fully clean model with consistent tax assumptions, both paths converge.

formulas.sensitivity_note: Both FCFE methods should reconcile to the same number in a properly built model. The advantage of building FCFE directly from Net Income is fewer steps and lower chance of arithmetic errors. The advantage of going via FCFF is that FCFF itself is useful for valuation purposes and is independent of leverage.
